 US flight chaos: Nearly 500 departures disrupted, thousands stranded as FAA halts take-offs nationwide; what we know so far 
 Trending Jensen Huang Chris Van Hollen Spain Protest Pakistan Accident Sheikh Hasina Nepal Accident US Iran War Jensen Huang Chris Van Hollen Spain Protest Pakistan Accident Sheikh Hasina Nepal Accident US Iran War Jensen Huang Chris Van Hollen Spain Protest Pakistan Accident Sheikh Hasina Nepal Accident US Iran War US flight chaos: Nearly 500 departures disrupted, thousands stranded as FAA halts take-offs nationwide; what we know so far 
 Edited by Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 14, 2026, 05:58 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print FAA issues national ground stop due to 'extraordinary circumstance and reasons for safety' Air travel across the United States was thrown into disruption on Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide halt to flight departures, citing a telecommunications outage affecting regional air traffic control centres. The unprecedented move grounded flights at airports across the country and disrupted travel plans for thousands of passengers, including people heading home, attending weddings and travelling for weekend events. The FAA said the restriction was imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”. The ground stop was the first nationwide suspension of flights since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and only the second such order since the September 11, 2001, attacks. Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said the outage appeared to be a telecommunications problem and that officials had no indication it was the result of an attack. However, the precise cause remained under investigation, with authorities examining the communications systems used by air traffic controllers. Here is what we know so far about the disruption, its possible cause and its impact on passengers. Why did the FAA ground flights across the US 
 The FAA ordered the nationwide ground stop after a communications problem affected the 22 regional air route traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft travelling between airports. Transportation secretary Sean Duffy said FAA technicians were investigating the issue. The agency described the decision as a safety measure, saying flights could not continue departing normally while the communications systems were affected. According to an airline source cited by CNN, the FAA told carriers that the outage was caused by a problem with network routers. The issue was believed to have originated at Chicago Midway International Airport before spreading across the country. The FAA was reportedly unable to provide a clear explanation of the problem during initial crisis discussions, with different facilities experiencing its effects in different ways. The ground stop meant aircraft could not take off, while planes already airborne were allowed to continue towards their destinations and land. Officials said they were handling flights still in the air on a case-by-case basis. Is the outage linked to a cyberattack or security threat? 
 US officials said there was no indication so far that the disruption was caused by a deliberate attack. US President Donald Trump said that the nationwide flight disruption was unlikely to have been caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence, as authorities investigated the telecommunications outage. Mullin told reporters at the White House that the problem was a telecommunications outage and not, based on the information available at the time, a hostile act against the country. "There was no indication as of yet this was a nefarious attack against us," he said. He added that officials were still investigating what had caused the outage and cautioned against making assumptions before the findings were available. He said there was no indication of a national security threat or deliberate attack. "This isn’t the same comparison to 9/11," he told reporters, adding that all flights had been accounted for and passengers were safe. "There is no indication that we’ve had, no reason to believe, that as of right now this was a threat to the United States," Mullin said, describing the incident as a telecommunications outage. He confirmed that Trump had been briefed and was coordinating with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and other officials. CNN, citing law enforcement sources, reported that preliminary assessments did not point to a cyberattack. A senior US security source later told the broadcaster that multiple law enforcement and intelligence agencies, including the FBI, Department of Homeland Security and National Security Agency, were examining the incident. The investigation was continuing to examine how the government's aviation systems connect to networks that could potentially be exposed to malicious actors. The senior security source said there was still no indication of an attack. Mullin also said officials were not ruling out any possibilities at the early stage of the investigation. Are the problems linked to the new FAA AI system or Microsoft outage? 
 Officials initially considered whether the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence-supported system could have contributed to the disruption. The system, known as SMART, analyses flight schedules, weather forecasts and other data from a location near Washington, DC. It then sends recommendations to the FAA's command centre and air traffic controllers. However, the system does not directly operate the regional air traffic control centres affected by Friday's communications outage. In a statement, ASI, the company that designed the system, said, "the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Mullin said officials had no indication that the new system was responsible for the disruption. He also said the outage was not connected to the major Microsoft services disruption reported earlier in the week. Microsoft separately said it had no indication that the FAA's nationwide ground stop was related to any of its services. How many flights have been affected 
 The disruption led to cancellations and delays at airports across the country, with further problems expected as the ground stop continued. According to aviation analytics company Cirium, nearly 481 flights had been cancelled or had failed to depart within 180 minutes of their scheduled departure time as of 4.40 pm Eastern time on Friday. This represented around 1.8% of the 26,284 flights scheduled to depart from US airports that day. Most of the affected departures at that stage were from airports in New York, San Francisco and Boston. Cirium said around 11,000 flights were scheduled to depart after 4 pm Eastern time, raising the prospect of further cancellations. The number of affected journeys increased as the hours-long suspension continued, leaving airlines and passengers trying to rearrange travel plans. The FAA's ground stop order was in effect until at least 11 pm Eastern time on Friday, although officials did not provide a definite timeline for restoring normal operations. Airlines cancel flights as FAA ground stop disrupts US travel 
 The nationwide ground stop prompted airlines to cancel services and warn passengers of further disruption. Air Canada said it had cancelled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of Friday evening because of the FAA restrictions. It also warned that flights between Canada, the Caribbean and South America that transit US airspace could be affected. JetBlue also planned to cancel the remainder of its flights on Friday, with the exception of services to Europe, according to a memo to pilots. The FAA had ordered the suspension after a temporary telecommunications outage affected all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centres, which guide aircraft travelling across the country. The agency said the measure was taken "out of an abundance of caution" and that international arrivals would be handled on a case-by-case basis. Flight-tracking platform FlightAware reported around 7,000 delayed or cancelled flights following the ground stop. Data from Flightradar24 showed that approximately 4,042 flights were airborne and heading towards US airports when the order was issued. What are airlines telling passengers? 
 Major US airlines warned customers to expect disruption and advised them to check flight information before travelling to airports. United Airlines said domestic flights would not depart during the suspension, while international departures were being handled by the FAA on a case-by-case basis. American Airlines said it expected disruption to continue for the rest of the day and that its teams would work to get passengers moving once the FAA lifted the restriction. The airline said: "It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this nationwide ground stop." Airports, including New York's John F Kennedy International Airport and LaGuardia Airport, also urged passengers to confirm their flight status with airlines before setting out. Passengers stranded as travel plans fall apart 
 The ground stop disrupted journeys at airports across the country, with passengers left uncertain about when they would be able to travel. At Chicago O'Hare International Airport, travellers discovered the disruption through departure screens showing widespread delays. Some contacted family members and friends while considering whether to book hotels or find alternative transport. Amber McQuilkin, a 27-year-old software engineer from Seattle, was concerned that she might miss a trip to New York for the League of Legends world finals after taking a week off work. Her friends had already reached the city. "There's not really any information being passed to me," she told news agency AP, adding that she had considered abandoning her flight and driving instead. Other passengers were forced to get off planes after boarding. Austin Curtis and his wife, travelling from South Bend, Indiana, to Denver for a friend's baby shower, were told to leave their aircraft at O'Hare after boarding their connecting flight. They were unsure whether to book a hotel or wait at the airport, with arrangements already made for the care of their two young children at home. The disruption also affected sporting travel. NBA, NHL and college teams were left uncertain about reaching destinations for weekend fixtures. Several college football teams, including Utah, Texas and Tennessee, were scheduled to travel for Saturday games. Why did the communications failure raise safety concerns? 
 Air traffic controllers rely on communication systems to direct aircraft travelling between airports. If those systems fail, controllers may not be able to communicate reliably with pilots, making it necessary to restrict new departures. Aviation safety expert and former United Airlines pilot Steve Arroyo told AP that Friday's incident appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communications outage in September that disrupted hundreds of flights across the northeastern US, but on a nationwide scale. "If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground," Arroyo said. "And not put them in the air where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them." Aviation professor Skip Bailey said that pilots are trained to respond if they lose radio contact with air traffic controllers. They are expected to maintain previously assigned headings and flight paths before reverting to their filed flight plans if the outage continues. Aircraft may also be able to communicate with one another. However, Bailey said preventing further departures was important to avoid adding aircraft to an already disrupted system. US air traffic control system faces modernisation challenges 
 The incident has renewed attention on the technology used by US air traffic controllers, much of which the government has been working to replace. Congress approved $12.5 billion for an overhaul last year. The programme includes replacing old copper wires with fibre-optic lines and gradually upgrading radio systems at airports. However, Transportation Secretary Duffy has said that another USD 30 billion would be needed to complete the modernisation effort. The White House has begun lobbying Congress for additional funding. Arroyo said Friday's outage could be linked to ageing technology, although officials had not established the cause. The disruption also had consequences beyond US airports. Eurocontrol's website showed that all US-bound traffic departing from its member states had been suspended at the FAA's request because of technical issues. Eurocontrol has 42 member states, including Israel. Despite the nationwide ground stop, SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday afternoon on its latest test flight. What happens next? 
 There was no confirmed timeline for the restoration of normal flight operations when officials addressed the disruption. Mullin said the immediate priority was ensuring that aircraft already in the air landed safely before services returned to normal. Join conversation

 The FAA and its technicians were continuing to investigate the communications failure, while US law enforcement and intelligence agencies examined whether any security-related factor was involved. For passengers, airlines and airports, the immediate advice was to check flight status directly with carriers before travelling. The scale and duration of the disruption would depend on how quickly the affected communications systems could be restored and normal departures resumed.
